title: Engaged Buddhism
hookLine: Thich Nhat Hanh and others bring practice to war, peace and daily life

lines: A BELL, AND SMOKE OVER A VILLAGE.
cards: A temple bell rings for evening sitting. Outside, not far off, there's the sound of planes, and smoke over a village. Inside the temple, young monks look at each other.
This was Vietnam during the war, and the question in that room was not abstract. Do you stay on the cushion, where the practice is? Or do you go out to the village, where the people are?
A monk named Thich Nhat Hanh spent his life answering that, and the answer gave a name to a whole movement.

teach.b: Thich Nhat Hanh was a Vietnamese Zen monk. As he told it later, when bombs were falling, monks and nuns had to choose between meditating in the monastery and going out to help the wounded.
He said they chose both. They rebuilt villages and cared for people, and kept their mindfulness while they did it, breathing as they carried the injured, walking with attention through the ruins.
He called this engaged Buddhism: practice that doesn't stop at the temple door. He started a school of young social workers who went into the villages.
He spoke against the war, was barred from going home, and lived much of his life in exile, teaching in France. He wasn't the only one.
Teachers in other countries have brought the practice into prisons, hospitals, protests, refugee camps and kitchens, each in their own way.

teach.h: NOT ONLY WHAT YOU DO, BUT HOW.
teach.b: Here's the turn that keeps it Buddhist: it isn't only what you do, but how. For Thich Nhat Hanh, anger at injustice was real, but acting from anger, he said, only adds more of the same to the world.
So the work starts inside: a breath before the meeting, attention while you wash the dishes, listening fully to someone you disagree with. Then you go out.
Not everyone in the tradition draws the lines the same way; some teachers keep monks far from politics, others step into it. But the root is old.
The Buddha taught that compassion, karuna, is one of the qualities a practitioner grows.
Engaged Buddhism asks where that compassion goes when you stand up from the cushion.

how: Engaged Buddhist groups run prison meditation programs, hospice care, disaster relief and peace work, and communities in the Plum Village tradition practice mindful breathing and walking alongside their service.

o: practice carried out into the world

s: engaged Buddhism is only about doing good deeds
it's also about how they're done: from calm and attention, not from anger.
Thich Nhat Hanh lived much of his life in exile
he spoke against the war and was barred from going home, and taught in France.
every Buddhist teacher agrees monks should be active in politics
some keep monks far from politics; others step in.

games.q: you're a young monk in Vietnam. the bombs are falling near a village. what do you do?
o: stay in the monastery and keep meditating
go out to help, and keep practicing while you do
leave the monastery and give up practice
games.why: as Thich Nhat Hanh told it, they chose both: they went out to help and tried to stay mindful while they worked.

practice: Choose one real thing that's wrong, in your house, your street, your town, small enough to hold, and notice what comes up: frustration, maybe tiredness. Breathe with that for a moment without pushing it away.
Then ask quietly what one thing you could do about it, from a calm place rather than an angry one, and let an answer come, or not.

wordCard.voice: Engaged Buddhism. Practice carried out of the temple and into war, peace and daily life, with attention to how the work is done.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit karuna: compassion, the wish for others to be free of suffering.

carryVoice: Your line: practice in the world. Not only what you do, but how. I'll be here tomorrow.
